nodes.statement: Suppose that $F$ contains the empty set and is closed under pairwise intersections and unions, and let $I$ be an $F$-capacity. Let $K$ be a compact system which is also closed under pairwise intersections. Let $s \in ((F \times K)^{\cup f})_\delta$. Then $\pi_{\mathcal{X}}(s) \in F_\delta$.
nodes.label: lem:mem_countableInfClosure_fst

nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a set of sets of $\mathcal{X}$ and let $I$ be an $F$-capacity. Suppose that $F$ contains the empty set and is closed under pairwise intersections and unions. Let $K$ be a compact system of $\mathcal{K}$ which is also closed under pairwise intersections. If a set $s$ of $\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{K}$ is capacitable with respect to the capacity $I_{\mathcal{X}}$ of Definition~\ref{def:Capacity.comp_fst}, then its projection on $\mathcal{X}$ is capacitable with respect to $I$.
nodes.label: lem:IsCapacitable.fst

nodes.name: Choquet's capacitability theorem
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a set of sets of $\mathcal{X}$ and let $I$ be an $F$-capacity. Suppose that $F$ contains the empty set and is closed under pairwise intersections and unions. Then every $F$-analytic set is $I$-capacitable.
nodes.label: thm:IsPavingAnalytic.isCapacitable

nodes.statement: Every finite measure defines a capacity by $I(s) = \mu(s)$ (where $\mu(s)$ is the value of the outer measure defined by $\mu$, but in Lean that's how $\mu(s)$ is defined already).
nodes.label: def:Measure.capacity

nodes.statement: A set is capacitable with respect to the capacity defined by a finite measure if and only if it is null-measurable for this measure.
nodes.label: lem:isCapacitable_measure_iff

nodes.statement: An $M_{\mathcal{X}}$-analytic set of a measurable space $\mathcal{X}$ is universally measurable: it is null-measurable for every finite measure on $\mathcal{X}$.
nodes.label: lem:IsPavingAnalytic.nullMeasurableSet

nodes.statement: A measurably analytic set of a measurable space $\mathcal{X}$ is universally measurable: it is null-measurable for every finite measure on $\mathcal{X}$.
nodes.label: lem:IsMeasurableAnalytic.nullMeasurableSet

nodes.name: Measurable projection
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Y}$ be measurable spaces, with $\mathcal{Y}$ standard Borel. Then the projection of a measurable set of $\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$ on $\mathcal{X}$ is universally measurable.
nodes.label: thm:MeasurableSet.nullMeasurableSet_fst

nodes.name: Monotone class
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{M}$ be a collection of subsets of a set $X$. We say that $\mathcal{M}$ is a monotone class if it is closed under countable monotone unions and countable monotone intersections, i.e.: \begin{enumerate} \item if \( A_1, A_2, \ldots \in M \) and \( A_1 \subseteq A_2 \subseteq \cdots \), then \( \bigcup_{i=1}^\infty A_i \in M \), \item if \( B_1, B_2, \ldots \in M \) and \( B_1 \supseteq B_2 \supseteq \cdots \), then \( \bigcap_{i=1}^\infty B_i \in M \). \end{enumerate} Given a collection $\mathcal{F}$ of subsets of $X$, we call the smallest monotone class containing $\mathcal{F}$ the monotone class generated by $\mathcal{F}$.
nodes.label: def:monotone_class

nodes.name: Monotone class theorem
nodes.statement: Let \(G\) be an algebra of subsets of a set \(X\). Then the monotone class generated by \(G\) coincides with the $\sigma$-algebra generated by \(G\).
nodes.label: thm:monotone_class

nodes.name: Progressively measurable set
nodes.statement: A subset of $[0, \infty) \times \Omega$ is progressively measurable if its indicator is a progressively measurable process.
nodes.label: def:progr_meas_set

nodes.name: Debut of a set
nodes.statement: Let $E \subseteq{} [0, \infty) \times \Omega $, define $D_E = \inf\left\lbrace t \geq 0\ :\ (t, \omega) \in E\right\rbrace$, the debut of $E$.
nodes.label: def:debut_set

nodes.statement: If $E$ is a progressively measurable set and the filtration satisfies the usual conditions, then $D_E$ is a stopping time.
nodes.label: thm:debut_of_progr_meas_is_stop_time

nodes.statement: If $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ is a progressively measurable process with respect to a filtration satisfying the usual conditions and $B$ is a Borel-measurable subset of $E$, then the hitting time of $X$ in $B$ is a stopping time.
nodes.label: thm:hitting_is_stopping_time

nodes.statement: Since $B$ is a Borel subset of $\mathcal{S}$ and $X$ is progressively measurable, then $\mathbf{1}_B(X_t)$ is also progressively measurable. The hitting time is then the debut of the set $E = \{(s,\omega) : \mathbf{1}_B(X_s(\omega)) = 1\}$, and therefore is a stopping time by Theorem~\ref{thm:debut_of_progr_meas_is_stop_time}.

Let $T$ be a conditionally complete linear order with a bottom element and let $R$ be a preorder. For a process $X : T \to Ω \to R$ and $a \in R$, define the random time \begin{align*} \tau_{X \ge a} = \inf\{t \in T \mid X_t \ge a\} \: , \end{align*} in which the infimum is infinite if the set is empty.
nodes.label: def:leastGE

nodes.statement: Let $T$ be a conditionally complete linear order with a bottom element, which is a Polish space for its order topology, on which we put the Borel $\sigma$-algebra. Let $R$ be a preorder with a metrizable topology for which sets of the form $\{x \in R \mid x \ge a\}$ are closed, with its Borel $\sigma$-algebra. If $X : T \to Ω \to R$ is a progressively measurable process with respect to a filtration satisfying the usual conditions, then for any $a \in R$, the random time $\tau_{X \ge a}$ is a stopping time.
nodes.label: lem:isStoppingTime_leastGE

nodes.statement: This is a direct application of Theorem~\ref{thm:hitting_is_stopping_time} with the set $B = [a, +\infty)$.

If $X : ι \to Ω \to ℝ$ is a right-continuous and adapted process with respect to a filtration satisfying the usual conditions, then for any $a \in \mathbb{R}$, the random time $\tau_{X \ge a}$ is a stopping time.
nodes.label: cor:isStoppingTime_leastGE_of_rightContinuous

nodes.statement: This follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:isStoppingTime_leastGE} since $X$ is progressively measurable by Lemma~\ref{lem:Adapted.isStronglyProgressive_of_rightContinuous}.

Let $T$ be a conditionally complete linear order with a bottom element and let $R$ be a preorder. For a process $X : T \to Ω \to R$ and $a \in R$, define the random time \begin{align*} \tau_{X > a} = \inf\{t \in T \mid X_t > a\} \: , \end{align*} in which the infimum is infinite if the set is empty.
nodes.label: def:leastGT

nodes.statement: Let $T$ be a conditionally complete linear order with a bottom element, which is a Polish space for its order topology, on which we put the Borel $\sigma$-algebra. Let $R$ be a preorder with a metrizable topology for which sets of the form $\{x \in R \mid x \ge a\}$ are closed, with its Borel $\sigma$-algebra. If $X : T \to Ω \to R$ is a progressively measurable process with respect to a filtration satisfying the usual conditions, then for any $a \in R$, the random time $\tau_{X > a}$ is a stopping time.
nodes.label: lem:isStoppingTime_leastGT

nodes.statement: This is a direct application of Theorem~\ref{thm:hitting_is_stopping_time} with the set $B = (a, +\infty)$.
For $t \in T$, $\tau_{X > a} < t$ if and only if there exists $s < t$ such that $X_s > a$.
nodes.label: lem:leastGT_lt_iff

nodes.statement: A pre-localizing sequence is a sequence of stopping times $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that $\tau_n \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$ (a.s.).
nodes.label: def:preLocalizingSequence

nodes.name: Localizing sequence
nodes.statement: A localizing sequence is a sequence of stopping times $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that $\tau_n$ is non-decreasing and $\tau_n \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$ (a.s.). That is, it is a pre-localizing sequence that is also almost surely non-decreasing.
nodes.label: def:localizingSequence

nodes.statement: The constant sequence $\tau_n = \infty$ is a localizing sequence.
nodes.label: lem:localizingSequence_const_top

nodes.statement: Let $(\sigma_n), (\tau_n)$ be localizing sequences. Then $(\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n)$ is a localizing sequence.
nodes.label: lem:localizingSequence_min

nodes.statement: If $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is a pre-localizing sequence, then the sequence defined by $\tau'_n = \inf_{m \ge n} \tau_m$ is a localizing sequence.
nodes.label: lem:isLocalizingSequence_of_isPreLocalizingSequence

nodes.statement: Let $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a localizing sequence and let $(\sigma_{n,k})_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a localizing sequence for each $n$. Then, there exists a strictly increasing sequence $(k_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that the sequence defined by $\tau'_n = \tau_n \wedge \sigma_{n,k_n}$ is a pre-localizing sequence.
nodes.label: lem:isPreLocalizingSequence_of_isLocalizingSequence

nodes.statement: For each $n$, since $\sigma_{n,k} \to \infty$ a.s. as $k \to \infty$, we may choose $k_n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $P(\sigma_{n,k_n} < \tau_n \wedge n) \le 2^{-n}$. Then, defining $\tau'_n = \tau_n \wedge \sigma_{n,k_n}$, we have $\tau_n' \to \infty$ by the Borel-Cantelli lemma.

Let $P$ be a predicate on paths and suppose $X$ is a stochastic process satisfying $P$ a.s. Then, defining $$\tau_n(\omega) = \begin{cases} \infty & \text{if } X(\omega) \text{ satisfies } P \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} $$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the sequence $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is a localizing sequence.
nodes.label: lem:isLocalizingSequence_ae

nodes.name: Local property
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be a class of stochastic processes (or equivalently a predicate on stochastic processes). We say that a stochastic process $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ is locally in $P$ (or satisfies $P$ locally) if there exists a localizing sequence $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the process $X^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0}$ is in $P$ (in which $X^{\tau_n}$ denotes the stopped process). We denote the class of processes that are locally in $P$ by $P_{\mathrm{loc}}$.
nodes.label: def:locally

nodes.statement: For any class of processes $P$, we have $P \subseteq P_{\mathrm{loc}}$.
nodes.label: lem:implies_locally

nodes.statement: Take $\tau_n = \infty$ for all $n$.
If $P \subseteq Q$ then $P_{\mathrm{loc}} \subseteq Q_{\mathrm{loc}}$.
nodes.label: lem:locally_mono

nodes.statement: Let $X \in P_{\mathrm{loc}}$. Then there exists a localizing sequence $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $X^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0} \in P$. Since $P \subseteq Q$, for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $X^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0} \in Q$. Thus $X \in Q_{\mathrm{loc}}$.
A class of stochastic processes $P$ is stable if whenever $X$ is in $P$, then for any stopping time $\tau$, the process $X^{\tau}\mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0}$ is also in $P$.
nodes.label: def:stable

nodes.statement: If $P$ is a stable class of processes, then $P_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is also stable.
nodes.label: lem:isStable_locally

nodes.statement: If $P, Q$ are stable classes of processes then $(P\cap Q)_{\mathrm{loc}} = P_{\mathrm{loc}}\cap Q_{\mathrm{loc}}$.
nodes.label: lem:locally_inter

nodes.statement: The forward direction is trivial so we only provide proof for the reverse. Suppose that $X \in P_{\mathrm{loc}}\cap Q_{\mathrm{loc}}$. Then, there exists localizing sequences $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ and $(\sigma_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that $X^{\tau_n} \mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0}\in P$ and $X^{\sigma_n} \mathbb{I}_{\sigma_n > 0} \in Q$. Consequently, by the stability of $P$, \[X^{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n} \mathbb{I}_{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n > 0} = (X^{\tau_n} \mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0})^{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n} \mathbb{I}_{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n > 0} \in P.\] Similarly, by the stability of $Q$, $X^{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n} \mathbb{I}_{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n > 0} \in Q$. Thus, as $\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n$ is a localizing sequence by Lemma~\ref{lem:localizingSequence_min} and $X^{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n} \mathbb{I}_{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n > 0} \in P \cap Q$ for all $n$, it follows that $X \in (P \cap Q)_{\mathrm{loc}}$

Let $P$ be a stable class of processes and let $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a pre-localizing sequence such that for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $X^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0}$ is in $P$. If the filtration is right-continuous, then $X$ is locally in $P$.
nodes.label: lem:locally_of_isPreLocalizingSequence

nodes.statement: Using the localizing sequence defined by Lemma~\ref{lem:isLocalizingSequence_of_isPreLocalizingSequence} suffices.
Suppose that the filtration is right-continuous. For any stable class of processes $P$, we have $(P_{\mathrm{loc}})_{\mathrm{loc}} = P_{\mathrm{loc}}$.
nodes.label: lem:locally_locally

nodes.statement: $(P_{\mathrm{loc}})_{\mathrm{loc}} \supseteq P_{\mathrm{loc}}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:isStable_locally} so we only prove the reverse inclusion. Let $X$ be a process in $(P_{\mathrm{loc}})_{\mathrm{loc}}$. By definition there exists a localizing sequence $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $X^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0}$ is in $P_{\mathrm{loc}}$. By definition of $P_{\mathrm{loc}}$, for each $n$ there exists a localizing sequence $(\sigma_{n,k})_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that for all $k \in \mathbb{N}$, $(X^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0})^{\sigma_{n,k}}\mathbb{I}_{\sigma_{n,k} > 0}$ is in $P$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:locally_of_isPreLocalizingSequence}, it suffices to show that there exists a pre-localizing sequence $(\tau'_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $X^{\tau'_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau'_n > 0}$ is in $P$. Thus, using the localizing sequences $\tau'_n = \tau_n \wedge \sigma_{n, k_n}$ defined by Lemma~\ref{lem:isPreLocalizingSequence_of_isLocalizingSequence}, it remains to argue that by stability of $P$, $X^{\tau'_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau'_n > 0}$ is in $P$ for all $n$. Indeed, this follows as $X^{\tau'_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau'_n > 0} = ((X^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0})^{\sigma_{n,k_n}}\mathbb{I}_{\sigma_{n,k_n} > 0})^{\tau'_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau'_n > 0}$ where $(X^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0})^{\sigma_{n,k_n}}\mathbb{I}_{\sigma_{n,k_n} > 0}$ is in $P$ by construction and $P$ is stable.

nodes.name: Local implication from global implication
nodes.statement: Suppose that the filtration is right-continuous. Let $P, Q$ be two classes of stochastic processes such that $P \subseteq Q_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and $Q$ is stable. Let $X$ be a stochastic process that satisfies $P$ locally. Then $X$ satisfies $Q$ locally. In short, if $P$ implies $Q$ locally, then $P$ locally implies $Q$ locally.
nodes.label: lem:local_induction

nodes.statement: Since $X \in P_{\mathrm{loc}}$, then $X \in (Q_{\mathrm{loc}})_{\mathrm{loc}}$ by assumption and Lemma~\ref{lem:locally_mono}. By Lemma \ref{lem:locally_locally}, $(Q_{\mathrm{loc}})_{\mathrm{loc}} = Q_{\mathrm{loc}}$. Thus $X \in Q_{\mathrm{loc}}$.
If $P$ be a predicate on paths such that the constant path $0$ satisfies $P$ and $X$ is a stochastic process satisfying $P$ a.s. then, $X$ satisfies $P$ locally.
nodes.label: lem:locally_of_ae

nodes.statement: Follows directly by using the localizing sequence defined in Lemma~\ref{lem:isLocalizingSequence_ae}.
A stochastic process $X$ is locally right continuous if and only if it is right continuous almost surely.
nodes.label: lem:locally_rightContinuous

nodes.statement: If $X$ is a.s. right continuous, then it is locally right continuous by Lemma~\ref{lem:locally_of_ae}. On the other hand, assuming $X$ is locally right continuous, there exists a localizing sequence $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\omega \in \Omega$, $(X^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0})(\omega)$ is right continuous. Thus, for almost surely every $\omega$ and any $t \in T$ there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $\tau_N(\omega) > t + 1$ (not that the ordering of a.s. and for all is important). Hence, as $X_s(\omega) = (X^{\tau_N}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_N > 0})_s(\omega)$ on a neighborhood of $t$, we have that $X(\omega)$ is right continuous at $t$. Consequently, as $t$ was arbitrary, $X$ is a.s. right continuous.
A stochastic process $X$ has left limits locally if and only if it has left limits almost surely.
nodes.label: lem:locally_leftLimit

nodes.statement: Same proof as in Lemma~\ref{lem:locally_rightContinuous}.
A stochastic process $X$ is locally cadlag if and only if it is cadlag almost surely.
nodes.label: lem:locally_isCadlag

nodes.statement: The forward direction follows from Lemmas~\ref{lem:locally_rightContinuous} and \ref{lem:locally_leftLimit} while the reverse direction follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:locally_of_ae}.
The class of right continuous processes is stable.
nodes.label: lem:isStable_rightContinuous

nodes.statement: Trivial.
The class of processes with left limits is stable.
nodes.label: lem:isStable_left_limit

nodes.statement: Trivial.
The class of cadlag processes is stable.
nodes.label: lem:isStable_isCadlag

nodes.statement: Follows from Lemmas~\ref{lem:isStable_rightContinuous} and \ref{lem:isStable_left_limit}.
The class of progressively measurable processes is stable.
nodes.label: lem:isStable_isStronglyProgressive

nodes.name: Local martingale
nodes.statement: We say a stochastic process $(M_t)_{t \in T}$ is a local martingale if it is locally a cadlag martingale in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:locally}. That is, there exists a localizing sequence $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the process $M^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0}$ is a cadlag martingale.
nodes.label: def:IsLocalMartingale

nodes.statement: A stochastic process is a local submartingale if it is locally a cadlag submartingale in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:locally}. That is, there exists a localizing sequence $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the process $M^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0}$ is a cadlag submartingale.
nodes.label: def:IsLocalSubmartingale

nodes.statement: Every cadlag martingale is a local martingale.
nodes.label: lem:Martingale.IsLocalMartingale

nodes.statement: This follows from Lemma \ref{lem:implies_locally}.
The class of cadlag martingales is stable. That is, if $M$ is a cadlag martingale and $\tau$ is a stopping time, then the stopped process cadlag $M^{\tau}\mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0}$ is also a martingale.
nodes.label: lem:stable_IsMartingale

nodes.statement: Clearly, the stopped process $M^{\tau}\mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0}$ is cadlag and it remains to show that it is a martingale. Fixing $s \le t \in T$, as $\{\tau > 0\} \in \mathcal{F}_0 \subseteq \mathcal{F}_s$, we have $$P[M^{\tau}_t \mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0} \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = \mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0}P[M_{\tau \wedge t} \mid \mathcal{F}_{s}].$$ Thus, as $\tau \wedge t$ is a bounded stopping time, we have by the optional stopping theorem (Lemma~\ref{lem:optionalSampling}) that $P[M_{\tau \wedge t} \mid \mathcal{F}_{s}] = M_{(\tau \wedge t) \wedge s} = M_{\tau \wedge s}$ and so, $P[M^{\tau}_t \mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0} \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = M^{\tau}_s \mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0}$ as required.

The class of cadlag submartingales is stable. That is, if $M$ is a cadlag submartingale and $\tau$ is a stopping time, then the stopped process $M^{\tau}\mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0}$ is also a cadlag submartingale.
nodes.label: lem:stable_IsSubmartingale

nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a continuous local martingale with $M_0 = 0$. If $M$ is also a finite variation process, then $M_t = 0$ for all $t$.
nodes.label: thm:IsLocalMartingale.eq_zero_of_finiteVariation

nodes.name: Integrable supremum
nodes.statement: We say that a stochastic process is integrable if the map $(t,\omega) \mapsto X_t(\omega)$ is strongly measurable and for all $t$, $X_t$ is integrable. A process has an integrable supremum if $(\sup_{s \le t} \Vert X_s \Vert)_t$ is integrable.
nodes.label: def:HasIntegrableSup

nodes.name: Locally integrable supremum
nodes.statement: A process has locally integrable supremum if it is locally a process with integrable supremum.
nodes.label: def:locallyIntegrableSup

nodes.name: Doob-Meyer class, class D
nodes.statement: A stochastic process $(X_t)$ is of class D (or in the Doob-Meyer class) if it is progressively measurable and the set $\{X_\tau \mid \tau \text{ is a finite stopping time}\}$ is uniformly integrable.
nodes.label: def:classD

nodes.name: Class DL
nodes.statement: A stochastic process $(X_t)$ is of class DL if it is progressively measurable and for all $t \ge 0$, the set $\{X_\tau \mid \tau \text{ is a stopping time with } \tau \le t\}$ is uniformly integrable.
nodes.label: def:classDL

nodes.statement: A stochastic process of class D is of class DL.
nodes.label: lem:classDLOfClassD

nodes.statement: This follows from the definitions and Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableComp}.
A stochastic process of class D is uniformly integrable.
nodes.label: lem:ClassD.uniformIntegrable

nodes.statement: Use the Class D property with the constant stopping times $\tau_n = n$ for all $n$ and apply Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableComp}.
A progressively measurable process is of class DL iff its norm is of class DL.
nodes.label: lem:classDL_iff_norm

nodes.statement: If a stochastic process is progressively measurable and the set \begin{align*} \{X_\tau \mid \tau \text{ is a stopping time and } \exists t, \forall \omega, \tau(\omega) \le t\} \end{align*} is uniformly integrable, then the process is of class D.
nodes.label: lem:classD_of_uniformIntegrable_bounded_stoppingTime

nodes.statement: A progressively measurable process is of class D iff its norm is of class D.
nodes.label: lem:classD_iff_norm

nodes.statement: Every nonnegative right-continuous submartingale is of class DL.
nodes.label: lem:Submartingale.classDL

nodes.statement: Let $t \in T$ and $\tau \le t$ be a stopping time. By Lemma~\ref{lem:optionalSamplingSubmartingale} and nonnegativity we get that $0 \le X_\tau \le P[X_t \mid X_\tau]$. As $X$ is a submartingale, $X_t$ is integrable, thus $\{X_t\}$ is uniformly integrable, and we can conclude from Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableDominated} and Lemma~\ref{lem:condExpUI}.
A nonnegative right-continuous submartingale is of class D if and only if it is uniformly integrable.
nodes.label: lem:Submartingale.classD_iff_uniformIntegrable

nodes.statement: Assume that $X$ is uniformly integrable. Just like what we did in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.classDL}, we use Lemma~\ref{lem:optionalSamplingSubmartingale} and Lemma~\ref{lem:condExpUI} to deduce that $\{X_\tau|\exists t\in T, \tau\le t\}$ is uniformly integrable. Moreover, for any finite stopping time $\tau$, We have that $X_\tau = \lim_{n \to +\infty} X_{\tau \land n}$. Thanks to Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrable_of_tendsto_ae}, we deduce that $X$ is of class D. Conversely, if $X$ is of class D, then it is uniformly integrable by Lemma~\ref{lem:ClassD.uniformIntegrable}.
Every càdlàg martingale is of class DL.
nodes.label: lem:Martingale.classDL

nodes.statement: Let $X$ be càdlàg martingale. By Lemma~\ref{lem:Martingale.submartingale_convex_comp}, $(|X_t|)_{t \in T}$ is a nonnegative càdlàg submartingale, and the result follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.classDL} along with Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableIffNorm}.
A right-continuous martingale is of class D if and only if it is uniformly integrable.
nodes.label: lem:Martingale.classD_iff_uniformIntegrable

nodes.statement: Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:classD_iff_norm} and Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableIffNorm}, it suffices to show the result for the norm of the martingale. That norm is a nonnegative right-continuous submartingale by Lemma~\ref{cor:Martingale.submartingale_norm} so this follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.classD_iff_uniformIntegrable}.
The class of processes for which the induced map $(t,\omega)\mapsto X_t(\omega)$ is strongly measurable is stable.
nodes.label: lem:isStable_stronglyMeasurable_uncurry

nodes.statement: The stopped process at $\tau$ is obtained by precomposition with $(t, \omega) \mapsto (\min (\tau(\omega), t), \omega)$. Precomposing a strongly measurable function with a measurable function gives a strongly measurable function. On a second-countable space, the minimum of two functions is measurable, and by assumption $\tau$ is measurable. The result follows from this.
The class of process with integrable supremum is stable.
nodes.label: lem:isStable_hasIntegrableSup

nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a process with integrable supremum and $\tau$ be a stopping time. Let $t \in T$. Then $(X^\tau)^*_t = \sup_{s \le t} \|X_{\tau \land s}\| \le \sup_{s \le t} \|X_s\| = X^*_t$, and as $X^*_t$ is integrable, so is $(X^\tau)^*_t$. Thus $(X^\tau \mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0})^*_t$ is integrable, concluding the proof.
The class of process with locally integrable supremum is stable.
nodes.label: lem:isStable_hasLocallyIntegrableSup

nodes.statement: Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:isStable_hasIntegrableSup} and Lemma~\ref{lem:isStable_locally}.
The class D is stable.
nodes.label: lem:isStable_classD

nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a process of class D and $\tau$ be a stopping time. For any finite stopping time $\sigma$, we have that $X_\sigma^\tau = X_{\sigma \land \tau}$. Because $\sigma \land \tau$ is finite and $X$ is of class D, we deduce from Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableComp} that $\{X_{\sigma \land \tau} \mid \sigma \text{ is a finite stopping time}\}$ is uniformly integrable, and thus that $\{X^\tau_\sigma \mid \sigma \text{ is a finite stopping time}\}$ is uniformly integrable. Using Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableDominated}, we obtain that $\{X^\tau_\sigma \mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0} \mid \sigma \text{ is a finite stopping time}\}$ is uniformly integrable, which concludes the proof.
The class DL is stable.
nodes.label: lem:isStable_classDL

nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a process of class DL, $\tau$ be a stopping time. Let $t \in T$. For any stopping time $\sigma \le t$, we have that $X_\sigma^\tau = X_{\sigma \land \tau}$. Because $\sigma \land \tau$ is bounded by $t$ and $X$ is of class DL, we deduce from Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableComp} that $\{X_{\sigma \land \tau} \mid \sigma \text{ is a stopping time with } \sigma \le t\}$ is uniformly integrable, and thus that $\{X^\tau_\sigma \mid \sigma \text{ is a stopping time with } \sigma \le t\}$ is uniformly integrable. Using Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableDominated}, we obtain that $\{X^\tau_\sigma \mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0} \mid \sigma \text{ is a stopping time with } \sigma \le t\}$ is uniformly integrable, which concludes the proof.
Let $X$ be a progressively measurable stochastic process with integrable supremum (Definition~\ref{def:HasIntegrableSup}). Then $X$ is of class DL.
nodes.label: lem:Integrable.classDL

nodes.statement: Let $t \in T$. For every stopping time $\tau$ with $\tau \le t$, we have $\|X_\tau\| \le X^*_t$. Measurability of $X_\tau$ follows from progressive measurability of $X$. Because by hypothesis $X^*_t$ is integrable, we deduce from Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableDominatedSingleton} that $\{X_\tau \mid \tau \text{ is a stopping time with } \tau \le t\}$ is uniformly integrable. This proves that $X$ is of class DL.
If the filtration satisfies the usual conditions, a progressively measurable process has a supremum that is jointly strongly measurable.
nodes.label: lem:IsStronglyProgressive.hasStronglyMeasurableSup

nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a progressively measurable stochastic process with locally integrable supremum. Then $X$ is locally of class DL.
nodes.label: lem:HasLocallyIntegrableSup.locally_classDL

nodes.statement: Combine Lemma~\ref{lem:Integrable.classDL} and Lemma~\ref{lem:locally_mono}. Use Lemma~\ref{lem:isStable_isStronglyProgressive} to get progressive measurability of the stopped processes.
If $X$ is of class DL then it is locally of class D.
nodes.label: lem:ClassDL.locally_classD

nodes.statement: Take $\tau_n := n$. Then \begin{align*} \{X^{\tau_n}_\sigma \mid \sigma \text{ is a finite stopping time}\} & = \{X_{\sigma \land n} \mid \sigma \text{ is a finite stopping time}\} \\ & \subseteq \{X_\sigma \mid \sigma \text{ is a stopping time with } \sigma \le n\}. \end{align*} Because $X$ is of class DL, that last set is uniformly integrable, thus $$\{X^{\tau_n}_\sigma \mid \sigma \text{ is a finite stopping time}\}$$ is uniformly integrable thanks to Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableComp}. Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableDominated} allows to conclude that $$\{X^{\tau_n}_\sigma \mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0} \mid \sigma \text{ is a finite stopping time}\}$$ is uniformly integrable, thus $X^{\tau_n} \mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0}$ is of class D. Obviously $\tau_n \rightarrow +\infty$ as $n$ goes to infinity, so $X$ is locally of class D.
If the filtration is right-continuous and $X$ is locally of class DL then it is locally of class D.
nodes.label: lem:locally_classD_of_locally_classDL

nodes.statement: Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:local_induction} using Lemma~\ref{lem:ClassDL.locally_classD} and Lemma~\ref{lem:isStable_classD}.
Assume $T$ is a linear order endowed with a topology making it first countable and $E$ is a pseudo-metric space. If $X$ is a càdlàg process then it maps compact sets of $T$ to bounded sets.
nodes.label: lem:isBounded_image_of_isCadlag_of_isCompact

nodes.statement: Let $K \subseteq T$ be a compact set and $\omega \in \Omega$. Assume that $X(\omega)(K)$ is not bounded. Then there exists a sequence $(t_n)$ in $K$ such that for all $n \in N$, $d(X_{t_n}(\omega), x) \ge n$, for some arbitrary $x \in E$. Because $K$ is compact, there is a subsequence $(t_{\phi(n)})$ that converges. Then one can extract a subsequence $(t_{\phi(\psi(n))})$ which either converges from below or from above. In both cases the sequence $(X_{t_{\phi(\psi(n))}})$ will converge, contradicting the hypotheses.

Assume $T$ has a bottom element and that its closed intervals are compact, and that the filtration is right-continuous. If $X$ is a real-valued càdlàg and adapted process, then the sequence $\tau_n := \inf \{t | X_t \ge n\}$ is a localizing sequence.
nodes.label: lem:isLocalizingSequence_leastGE

nodes.statement: By Corollary~\ref{cor:isStoppingTime_leastGE_of_rightContinuous}, each $\tau_n$ is a stopping time. Moreover, for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $X_t \ge n+1 \implies X_t \ge n$, thus $\tau_n \le \tau_{n+1}$. Finally, for every $\omega \in \Omega$ and $t_0 \in T$ there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for all $s \le t_0$, $X_s \le N$ thanks to Lemma~\ref{lem:isBounded_image_of_isCadlag_of_isCompact}. Thus for all $n \ge N$, $\tau_n(\omega) \ge t_0$, proving that $\tau_n$ tends to infinity as n goes to infinity.

For $Y$ a stochastic process, let $Y^*_t = \sup_{s \le t} \Vert Y_s \Vert$. Let $X$ be a stochastic process and let $\tau = \inf \{t \mid \Vert X_t \Vert \ge n\}$ for some $n \in \mathbb{R}$. Then \begin{align*} (X^{\tau})^*_t \le n + \mathbb{1}_{\tau \le t} \Vert X_{\tau} \Vert \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:sup_stoppedProcess_le

nodes.statement: If $\tau > t$, then for all $s \le t$, $\|X_s\| \le n$, and thus $(X^\tau)^*_t = \sup_{s \le t} \|X_{\tau \land s}\| \le n = n + \mathbb{1}_{\tau \le t} \|X_{\tau}\|$. Otherwise $(X^\tau)^*_t = \sup_{s \le \tau} \|X_s\|$. For $s < \tau$, $\|X_s\| \le n$, and $\|X_\tau\| \le \|X_\tau\|$ so $\sup_{s \le \tau} \|X_s\| \le n \lor \|X_\tau\| \le n + \|X_\tau\| = n + \mathbb{I}_{\tau \le t} \|X_\tau\|$.

Assume $T$ has a bottom element and that its closed intervals are compact, and that the filtration is right-continuous. If $X$ is a càdlàg process of class DL, then it has locally integrable supremum.
nodes.label: lem:ClassDL.hasLocallyIntegrableSup

nodes.statement: Set $\tau_n := \inf \{t | X_t \ge n\}$. This is a localizing sequence by Lemma~\ref{lem:isLocalizingSequence_leastGE}. For every $t \in T$, we have by Lemma~\ref{lem:sup_stoppedProcess_le} that $(X^{\tau_n})^*_t \le n + \mathbb{I}_{\tau_n \le t} \|X_{\tau_n}\| = n + \mathbb{I}_{\tau_n \le t} \|X_{\tau_n \land t}\|$. Because X is of class DL, $X_{\tau_n \land t}$ is integrable, so $(X^{\tau_n})^*_t$ is integrable too, so $(X^{\tau_n} \mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0})^*_t$ is integrable. Thus $X$ has locally integrable supremum.

Assume $T$ has a bottom element and that its closed intervals are compact. Assume that the filtration is right-continuous. If a process is càdlàg and locally of class DL, then it has locally integrable supremum.
nodes.label: lem:hasLocallyIntegrableSup_of_locally_classDL

nodes.statement: Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:local_induction} using Lemma~\ref{lem:ClassDL.hasLocallyIntegrableSup} and Lemma~\ref{lem:isStable_hasIntegrableSup}.

Assume $T$ has a bottom element and that its closed intervals are compact, and that the filtration is right-continuous. If $X$ is a càdlàg process, then it is locally of class DL if and only if it has locally integrable supremum.
nodes.label: lem:locally_classDL_iff_locallyIntegrableSup

nodes.statement: The two directions are proved in Lemmas~\ref{lem:hasLocallyIntegrableSup_of_locally_classDL} and \ref{lem:HasLocallyIntegrableSup.locally_classDL}.

Assume $T$ has a bottom element and that its closed intervals are compact, and that the filtration is right-continuous. A càdlàg process is locally of class D if and only if it is locally of class DL.
nodes.label: lem:locally_classD_iff_locally_classDL

nodes.statement: The forward direction follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:classDLOfClassD} along with Lemma~\ref{lem:locally_mono}. The reverse direction is Lemma~\ref{lem:locally_classD_of_locally_classDL}.

Assume $T$ has a bottom element and that its closed intervals are compact, and that the filtration is right-continuous. A càdlàg process is locally of class D if and only if it has locally integrable supremum.
nodes.label: lem:locally_classD_iff_locallyIntegrableSup

nodes.statement: This follows from Lemmas~\ref{lem:locally_classD_iff_locally_classDL} and \ref{lem:locally_classDL_iff_locallyIntegrableSup}.
Every cadlag submartingale for a right-continuous filtration has locally integrable supremum.
nodes.label: lem:Submartingale.locallyIntegrableSup

nodes.statement: Define the stopping times $\sigma_n = \inf\{t \mid \Vert X_t \Vert \ge n\}$ and set $\tau_n = \sigma_n \wedge n$. $\sigma_n$ is a stopping time by Lemma~\ref{cor:isStoppingTime_leastGE_of_rightContinuous} and so $\tau_n$ is also a stopping time. The times $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ form a localizing sequence. By Lemma~\ref{lem:sup_stoppedProcess_le}, we have that \begin{align*} (X^{\tau_n})^*_t & \le n + \mathbb{1}_{\tau_n \le t} \Vert X_{\tau_n} \Vert \\ & \le n + \Vert X_{\tau_n} \Vert \: . \end{align*} It remains to show that $X_{\tau_n}$ is integrable for each $n$. This follows by Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.integrable_stoppedValue} as $\tau_n$ is a bounded stopping time.
Every cadlag submartingale is locally of class D.
nodes.label: lem:Submartingale.locally_classD

nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:locally_classD_iff_locally_classDL}, it suffices to show that every cadlag submartingale is locally of class DL. This can be proved with Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.classDL}.
Every local submartingale is locally of class D.
nodes.label: lem:IsLocalSubmartingale.locally_classD

nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:local_induction}, it suffices to show that if $X$ is a submartingale then it is locally of class D. This is done in Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.locally_classD}.
Every local martingale is locally of class D.
nodes.label: lem:IsLocalMartingale.locally_classD

nodes.statement: A local martingale is a cadlag martingale if and only if it is of class DL.
nodes.label: lem:IsLocalMartingale.martingale_iff_classDL

nodes.statement: A nonnegative local submartingale is a cadlag submartingale if and only if it is of class DL.
nodes.label: lem:IsLocalSubmartingale.submartingale_iff_classDL_of_nonnegative

nodes.name: Semi-ring of sets
nodes.statement: A \emph{semi-ring of sets} $C$ is a family of sets containing $\emptyset$, stable by intersection and such that for all $s, t \in C$, $s \setminus t$ is equal to a disjoint union of finitely many sets in $C$~.
nodes.label: def:semiRingOfSets

nodes.statement: The family of intervals of the form $(s, t]$ with $s < t$ in a linear order $T$ is a semi-ring of sets.
nodes.label: lem:semiRingOfSets_of_intervals

nodes.statement: Suppose that $C$ is a semi-ring of sets, and let $A_k \in C$, $k \in \{1, ..., n\}$~. Then there exists a family of pairwise disjoint sets $B_j \in C$, $j \in \{1, ..., m\}$, such that $\bigcup_{k=1}^n A_k = \bigcup_{j=1}^m B_j$~.
nodes.label: lem:semiRingOfSets_disjoint_of_union

nodes.statement: Suppose that $C$ is a semi-ring of sets, and let $A_k \in C$, $k \in \{1, ..., n\}$, and $B\in C$~. Then there exists a family of pairwise disjoint sets $B_j \in C$, $j \in \{1, ..., m\}$, such that \[ B\setminus\bigcup_{k=1}^n A_k = \bigcup_{j=1}^m B_j. \]
nodes.label: cor:semiRingOfSets_subtractUnion

nodes.statement: This is easily done by induction on $n$, thanks to the Lemma~\ref{lem:semiRingOfSets_disjoint_of_union}.

The family of pairwise disjoint sets $B_j$ in the Lemma~\ref{lem:semiRingOfSets_disjoint_of_union} can be chosen as a refinement of the family $(A_k)$, that is, for every $k$ and $j$, $B_j \cap A_k \in \{\emptyset, B_j\}$~.
nodes.label: lem:semiRingOfSets_disjoint_of_union_finer

nodes.statement: TODO: The construction in Lean, \begin{verbatim} MeasureTheory.IsSetSemiring.disjointOfUnion_props \end{verbatim} lacks this property; indeed, for $J = \{ (1,3], (0,2] \}$ (in this order), the algorithm produces $K (1,3] = (1,3]$ and then $K (0,2] = (0,1]$ (the latter being a finite partition of the difference $(0,2]\setminus(1,3]$); but the intersection of $B_1=(1,3]$ and $A_2=(0,2]$ is neither empty, nor the $B_1$~. An enhancement of that algorithm could consist in taking $K_1 t$, $t\neq s$, to be \[ \{ u\cap s \mid u\in (K t)\} \cup \{ v \mid v\in d(u,s),\; u\in (K t)\}, \] where $d(u,s)$ denotes the chosen disjoint family of elements of $C$, whose union is $u\setminus s$~.

nodes.name: Ring of sets
nodes.statement: A \emph{ring of sets} $C$ is a family of sets containing $\emptyset$, stable by union and set difference (and thus also by intersection).
nodes.label: def:ringOfSets

nodes.statement: If $C$ is a semi-ring of sets, then finite unions of elements of $C$ form a ring of sets, $D$~. We call $D$ the ring generated by $C$~.
nodes.label: lem:setRing_of_finiteUnions

nodes.statement: Suppose that $D$ is a ring of sets, generated by the semi-ring $C$~. If $A\in D$ and $B\in C$, then there exists a family of pairwise disjoint sets $B_j \in C$, $j \in \{1, ..., m\}$, such that \[ B\setminus A = \bigcup_{j=1}^m B_j. \]
nodes.label: cor:semiRingOfSets_subtract_ringElem

nodes.statement: This is just another wording of the Corollary~\ref{cor:semiRingOfSets_subtractUnion}, thanks to the Lemma~\ref{lem:setRing_of_finiteUnions}.

nodes.name: Predictable rectangles
nodes.statement: The class of \emph{predictable rectangles} on $T \times \Omega$ is \begin{align*} \mathcal{R}_T := \big\{(s, t] \times F : s, t \in T,\ s < t,\ F \in \mathcal{F}_s\big\} \cup \big\{\{0\} \times F : F \in \mathcal{F}_0\big\} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 10.2 Simple processes and elementary predictable sets
nodes.label: def:predictableRectangles

nodes.statement: The class $\mathcal{R}_T$ of predictable rectangles is a semi-ring of sets.
nodes.section: 10.2 Simple processes and elementary predictable sets
nodes.label: lem:predictableRectangles_isSetSemiring

nodes.statement: Take two elements $A, B \in \mathcal{R}_T$~. If only one of $A, B$ is of the form $\{0\} \times F$, they are disjoint, so both the intersection and the difference are trivially in $\mathcal{R}_T$~. If both are of this form, then $A\cap B$, $A\setminus B\in\mathcal{R}_T$ follows from the fact that $\mathcal{F}_0$ is a $\sigma$-algebra. Let then $A=(s, t] \times F$ and $B=(s', t'] \times F'$~. We shall understand $(s,t]$ as the empty set if $s \ge t$~. Both $F \cap F'$ and $F \setminus F'$ are in $\mathcal{F}_{s \vee s'}$~. It is now clear that $A\cap B$ is a predictable rectangle, since \[ A \cap B = (s \vee s', t \wedge t'] \times (F \cap F'). \] Finally, let $I=(s,t]$ and $J=(s',t']$. Then \[ (I\times F)\setminus(J\times F') = ((I\setminus J)\times F) \cup ((I\cap J)\times(F\setminus F')). \] The union is disjoint, and \[ I\setminus J = (s,t\wedge s']\cup(s\vee t',t]. \] Hence $A\setminus B$ is a disjoint union of at most three predictable rectangles. Indeed, $F\in\mathcal{F}_{s\vee t'}$ by monotonicity of the filtration, and $F\setminus F'\in\mathcal{F}_{s\vee s'}$ as noted earlier.
nodes.section: 10.2 Simple processes and elementary predictable sets

nodes.name: Elementary predictable set
nodes.statement: A set $A \subseteq T \times \Omega$ is an \emph{elementary predictable set} if it is a finite union of sets of the form ${0} \times B$ for $B \in \mathcal{F}_0$ or of the form $(s, t] \times B$ with $0 \le s < t$ in $T$ and $B \in \mathcal{F}_s$~.
nodes.section: 10.2 Simple processes and elementary predictable sets
nodes.label: def:elementaryPredictableSet

nodes.statement: Every elementary predictable set (Definition~\ref{def:elementaryPredictableSet}) is a finite union of predictable rectangles.
nodes.section: 10.2 Simple processes and elementary predictable sets
nodes.label: lem:predictableRectangles_generate_elementaryPredictableSets

nodes.statement: This follows immediately from the definitions.
nodes.section: 10.2 Simple processes and elementary predictable sets

nodes.statement: The family of elementary predictable sets (Definition~\ref{def:elementaryPredictableSet}) is a ring of sets, the one generated by the semi-ring of predictable rectangles.
nodes.section: 10.2 Simple processes and elementary predictable sets
nodes.label: lem:elementaryPredictableSets_isSetRing_of

nodes.statement: Since elementary predictable sets are finite unions of predictable rectangles (Lemma~\ref{lem:predictableRectangles_generate_elementaryPredictableSets}), the claim follows by Lemma~\ref{lem:setRing_of_finiteUnions}.
nodes.section: 10.2 Simple processes and elementary predictable sets

nodes.statement: Any elementary predictable set (Definition~\ref{def:elementaryPredictableSet}) is a disjoint union of predictable rectangles.
nodes.section: 10.2 Simple processes and elementary predictable sets
nodes.label: lem:elementaryPredictableSets_asDisjointUnions

nodes.statement: Since elementary predictable sets are finite unions of predictable rectangles (Lemma~\ref{lem:predictableRectangles_generate_elementaryPredictableSets}), which form a semi-ring of sets (Lemma~\ref{lem:predictableRectangles_isSetSemiring}), the claim follows by Lemma~\ref{lem:semiRingOfSets_disjoint_of_union}.
nodes.section: 10.2 Simple processes and elementary predictable sets

nodes.statement: An elementary predictable set is measurable with respect to the predictable $\sigma$-algebra.
nodes.section: 10.2 Simple processes and elementary predictable sets
nodes.label: lem:predictableSet_elementaryPredictableSet

nodes.statement: It is a union of sets of the form ${0} \times B$ with $B \in \mathcal{F}_0$ or of the form $(s, t] \times B$ with $B \in \mathcal{F}_s$, which are measurable by Lemma~\ref{lem:predictable_Ioc_prod}.
nodes.section: 10.2 Simple processes and elementary predictable sets

nodes.name: Simple process
nodes.statement: Let $(s_k < t_k)_{k \in \{1, ..., n\}}$ be points in a linear order $T$ with a bottom element 0. Let $(\eta_k)_{0 \le k \le n}$ be bounded random variables with values in a normed real vector space $E$ such that $\eta_0$ is $\mathcal{F}_0$-measurable and $\eta_k$ is $\mathcal{F}_{s_k}$-measurable for $k \ge 1$~. Then the simple process for that sequence is the process $V : T \to \Omega \to E$ defined by \begin{align*} V_t = \eta_0 \mathbb{1}_{\{0\}}(t) + \sum_{k=1}^{n} \eta_k \mathbb{1}_{(s_k, t_k]}(t) \: . \end{align*} Let $\mathcal{E}_{T, E}$ be the set of simple processes indexed by $T$ with value in $E$.
nodes.section: 10.2 Simple processes and elementary predictable sets
nodes.label: def:simpleProcess

nodes.statement: The definition of simple process does not change if we require the intervals $(s_k, t_k]$ to be disjoint.
nodes.section: 10.2 Simple processes and elementary predictable sets
nodes.label: lem:simpleProcess_admitsDisjointIntervals

nodes.statement: Fix a simple process $V$. The union of its time intervals is $A=\bigcup_{k=1}^n A_k$ with $A_k = (s_k, t_k]$~. Intervals of this type form a semi-ring of sets (Lemma~\ref{lem:semiRingOfSets_of_intervals}), so we may use the Lemma~\ref{lem:semiRingOfSets_disjoint_of_union_finer} to write $A$ as a disjoint union of intervals $B_j=(u_j, v_j]$, where for each $j$ and $k$, \[ B_j \cap A_k \in \{\emptyset, B_j\}. \] For each $j$, we then construct the random variable $\xi_j$ by summing the $\eta_k$'s for which $B_j \subseteq A_k$; as $s_k\le u_j$ in that case, $\xi_j$ is $\mathcal{F}_{u_j}$-measurable. Each $B_j$ is either disjoint from an $A_k$ or contained in it, which justifies \begin{align*} V_t &= \eta_0 \mathbb{1}_{\{0\}}(t) + \sum_{k=1}^{n} \eta_k \mathbb{1}_{A_k}(t) = \eta_0 \mathbb{1}_{\{0\}}(t) + \sum_{j=1}^{m} \xi_j \mathbb{1}_{B_j}(t) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 10.2 Simple processes and elementary predictable sets

nodes.statement: A simple process is predictable.
nodes.section: 10.2 Simple processes and elementary predictable sets
nodes.label: lem:predictable_simpleProcess

nodes.section: 10.2 Simple processes and elementary predictable sets

nodes.statement: Real simple processes generate the predictable $\sigma$-algebra, i.e., the predictable $\sigma$-algebra is the supremum of the comaps by simple processes (seen as maps from $T \times \Omega$ to $\mathbb{R}$) of the Borel $\sigma$-algebra.
nodes.section: 10.2 Simple processes and elementary predictable sets
nodes.label: lem:iSup_comap_simpleProcess

nodes.section: 10.2 Simple processes and elementary predictable sets

nodes.statement: A set $A \subseteq T \times \Omega$ is an elementary predictable set if and only if the indicator function $\mathbb{1}_A$ is a simple process.
nodes.section: 10.2 Simple processes and elementary predictable sets
nodes.label: lem:elementaryPredictableSet_iff_indicator

nodes.statement: Suppose that $A$ is an elementary predictable set; by Lemma~\ref{lem:elementaryPredictableSets_asDisjointUnions}, $A$ is a disjoint union of predictable rectangles. In other words, $\mathbb{1}_A$ is a sum of indicator functions of predictable rectangles, and thus a simple process. In the other direction, suppose $\mathbb{1}_A$ is a simple process, \[ \mathbb{1}_A(t,\cdot) = \eta_0 \mathbb{1}_{\{0\}}(t) + \sum_{k=1}^{n} \eta_k \mathbb{1}_{(s_k, t_k]}(t). \] By Lemma~\ref{lem:simpleProcess_admitsDisjointIntervals}, we can assume that $(s_k, t_k]$ are pairwise disjoint; then each of $\eta_1$, \dots, $\eta_n$ must be an indicator function, \[ \eta_k = \mathbb{1}_{F_k}, \quad\text{with } F_k \in \mathcal{F}_{s_k}, \] and $\eta_0 = \mathbb{1}_{F_0}$ for some $F_0 \in \mathcal{F}_0$~. This shows that $A$ is a finite union of predictable rectangles, and thus an elementary predictable set.
nodes.section: 10.2 Simple processes and elementary predictable sets

nodes.statement: The simple processes $\mathcal{E}_{T, F}$ form an additive commutative group.
nodes.section: 10.2 Simple processes and elementary predictable sets
nodes.label: lem:addCommGroup_simpleProcess

nodes.section: 10.2 Simple processes and elementary predictable sets

nodes.statement: The simple processes $\mathcal{E}_{T, F}$ form a module over the scalars $\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.section: 10.2 Simple processes and elementary predictable sets
nodes.label: lem:module_simpleProcess

nodes.section: 10.2 Simple processes and elementary predictable sets

nodes.name: Elementary stochastic integral
nodes.statement: Let $V \in \mathcal{E}_{T, E}$ be a simple process and let $X$ be a stochastic process with values in a normed space $F$. Let $B$ be a continuous bilinear map from $E \times F$ to another normed space $G$. The \emph{general elementary stochastic integral} process $V \bullet_B X : T \to \Omega \to G$ is defined by \begin{align*} (V \bullet_B X)_t &= \sum_{k=1}^{n} B (\eta_k, X^t_{t_k} - X^t_{s_k}) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: def:elemStochIntegralBilin

nodes.statement: For $V, W$ two simple processes with values in $E$ and $F$ respectively, the process defined by $B(V, W)_t(\omega) = B(V_t(\omega), W_t(\omega))$ is a simple process. Note: in Lean, the above is not a lemma but a definition of a simple process with a lemma that its coercion to a function is given by above.
nodes.label: lem:simpleProcess_map2

nodes.statement: It has values $B(\eta_i, \xi_j)$ on the intervals $(s_i, t_i] \cap (u_j, v_j]$ if $V$ and $W$ are defined by the sequences $(s_i, t_i, \eta_i)$ and $(u_j, v_j, \xi_j)$ respectively.

Let $E$ and $F$ be normed real vector spaces. We call \emph{linear elementary stochastic integral} the general elementary stochastic integral of Definition~\ref{def:elemStochIntegralBilin} with $V$ being valued in $L(E, F)$-valued and $B(L, x) = L(x)$ the evaluation map. We denote it by $V \bullet_L X$, or just $V \bullet X$ when $L$ is clear from the context.
nodes.label: def:elemStochIntegralLinear

nodes.statement: We call \emph{scalar elementary stochastic integral} the general elementary stochastic integral of Definition~\ref{def:elemStochIntegralBilin} with $V$ being $\mathbb{R}$-valued and $B(r, x) = r \cdot x$ the scalar multiplication. We denote it by $V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X$.
nodes.label: def:elemStochIntegral

nodes.statement: The elementary stochastic integrals $\bullet_B$, $\bullet_L$ and $\bullet_{\mathbb{R}}$ are linear in both arguments.
nodes.label: lem:elemStochIntegral_linear

nodes.statement: (In Lean, this is split into several lemmas about each argument and add/sub/smul.) Immediate from the definition.
$(V \bullet_B X)_0 = 0$ for every simple process $V$ and stochastic process $X$.
nodes.label: lem:elemStochIntegralBilin_zero

nodes.statement: \begin{align*} (V \bullet_B X)_0 &= \sum_{k=1}^{n} B (\eta_k, X^0_{t_k} - X^0_{s_k}) \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^{n} B (\eta_k, X_{0} - X_{0}) \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^{n} B (\eta_k, 0) \\ &= 0 \: . \end{align*}
Let $X_c$ be a constant process (equal to the same random variable for all times). Then for every simple process $V$, \begin{align*} V \bullet_B X_c = 0 \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:elemStochIntegralBilin_const

nodes.statement: Let $E, F, G, H, I, J$ be normed real vector spaces. Let $B_1 : E \times H \to I$, $B_2 : F \times G \to H$, $B_3 : E \times F \to J$ and $B_4 : J \times G \to I$ be continuous bilinear maps such that for all $x \in E$, $y \in F$ and $z \in G$, $B_1(x, B_2(y, z)) = B_4(B_3(x, y), z)$. Then for every simple process $V$ with values in $E$, simple process $W$ with values in $F$, and stochastic process $X$ with values in $G$, we have \begin{align*} V \bullet_{B_1} (W \bullet_{B_2} X) &= B_3(V, W) \bullet_{B_4} X \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:elemStochIntegralBilin_assoc

nodes.statement: Unfold definitions, use linearity.

Let $E, F, G$ be normed real vector spaces. Let $B : E \times F \to G$ be a continuous bilinear map. Then for every simple process $V$ with values in $\mathbb{R}$, simple process $W$ with values in $E$, and stochastic process $X$ with values in $F$, we have \begin{align*} V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} (W \bullet_{B} X) &= (V \cdot W) \bullet_{B} X \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: cor:elemStochIntegral_assoc_real_bilin

nodes.statement: Use Lemma~\ref{lem:elemStochIntegralBilin_assoc}.
$V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} (W \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X) = (V \times W) \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X$ for real-valued simple processes $V, W$ and stochastic process $X$.
nodes.label: lem:elemStochIntegral_assoc

nodes.statement: Apply Corollary~\ref{cor:elemStochIntegral_assoc_real_bilin} with $B$ the scalar multiplication.

For simple process $W$ with values in $L(E, F)$, simple process $V$ with values in $L(F, G)$, and stochastic process $X$ with values in $E$, we have \begin{align*} V \bullet_L (W \bullet_L X) &= (V \circ W) \bullet_L X \: , \end{align*} in which $V \circ W$ is the simple process defined by $(V \circ W)_t = V_t \circ W_t$.
nodes.label: lem:elemStochIntegralLinear_assoc

nodes.statement: Use Lemma~\ref{lem:elemStochIntegralBilin_assoc} with $B_1, B_2, B_4$ equal to the evaluation maps and $B_3$ the composition of continuous linear maps.
For $V \in \mathcal{E}_{T, F}$, $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ a càdlàg process and a continuous bilinear map $B: E \times F \to G$, the elementary stochastic integral $V \bullet_B X$ is càdlàg.
nodes.label: lem:cadlag_elemStochIntegralBilin

nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a stochastic process, $V$ a simple process and $τ$ a stopping time. Then \begin{align*} (V \bullet_B X)^τ = V \bullet_B (X^τ) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:elemStochIntegral_stoppedProcess

nodes.statement: \begin{align*} (V \bullet_B X)^\tau_t &= (V \bullet_B X)_{t \wedge \tau} \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^{n} B (\eta_k, X^{t \wedge \tau}_{t_k} - X^{t \wedge \tau}_{s_k}) \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^{n} B (\eta_k, (X^{\tau})^t_{t_k} - (X^{\tau})^t_{s_k}) \\ &= (V \bullet_B (X^{\tau}))_t \: . \end{align*}

Let $X$ be a stochastic process and $τ$ be a stopping time taking finitely many values. Then $\mathbb{1}_{[0, τ]}$ is a simple process and \begin{align*} X^τ = X_0 + \mathbb{1}_{[0, τ]} \bullet X \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:stoppedProcess_eq_elemStochIntegral

nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a stochastic process, $V$ a real-valued simple process, and $τ$ a stopping time taking finitely many values. Then \begin{align*} (V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)^τ = (\mathbb{1}_{[0,τ]}V) \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:elemStochIntegral_stoppedIntegrator

nodes.statement: Replace, in the formula (Lemma~\ref{lem:elemStochIntegral_stoppedProcess}): \[ (V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)^τ = V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} (X^τ), \] the $X^\tau$ by $X_0 + \mathbb{1}_{[0, τ]} \bullet X$ using Lemma~\ref{lem:stoppedProcess_eq_elemStochIntegral}. Now, $X_0$ may be dropped in the resulting integral, by linearity (Lemma~\ref{lem:elemStochIntegral_linear}) and Lemma~\ref{lem:elemStochIntegralBilin_const}, that is, \[ (V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)^τ = V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} (\mathbb{1}_{[0, τ]} \bullet X). \] Application of Corollary~\ref{cor:elemStochIntegral_assoc_real_bilin} gives the desired result.
For $V$ a simple process and $X$ a stochastic process, $(V \bullet_B X)_t$ tends to its limit process $(V \bullet_B X)_\infty$ as $t$ goes to infinity.
nodes.label: lem:tendsto_elemStochIntegral_limitProcess

nodes.statement: That process is eventually constant.
\begin{align*} (V \bullet_B X)_\infty &= \sum_{k=1}^{n} B (\eta_k, X_{t_k} - X_{s_k}) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:limitProcess_elemStochIntegral

nodes.statement: Immediate from the definition.

An adapted integrable process $X$ is a submartingale if and only if for every bounded simple process $V$ with values in $\mathbb{R}_+$, $\mathbb{E}[(V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)_\infty] \ge 0$. Note that in Lean $V$ comes with the data of a sum representation: by ``values in $\mathbb{R}_+$'' we mean that the random variables in that particular sum representing $V$ are nonnegative.
nodes.label: lem:submartingale_iff_integral_elemStochIntegral_nonneg

nodes.statement: First suppose that $X$ is a submartingale. The simple process $V$ can be written as $V_t = \eta_0 \mathbb{1}_{\{0\}}(t) + \sum_{k=1}^{n} \eta_k \mathbb{1}_{(s_k, t_k]}(t)$ for nonnegative $\eta_k$. Then \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[(V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)_\infty] &= \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{k=1}^{n} \eta_k (X_{t_k} - X_{s_k})\right] \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^{n} \mathbb{E}[\eta_k (X_{t_k} - X_{s_k})] \: . \end{align*} It suffices to show that each term of the sum is nonnegative. Since $\eta_k$ is $\mathcal{F}_{s_k}$-measurable and nonnegative, by the submartingale property we have \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[\eta_k (X_{t_k} - X_{s_k})] &= \mathbb{E}[\eta_k \mathbb{E}[X_{t_k} - X_{s_k} \mid \mathcal{F}_{s_k}]] \ge 0 \: . \end{align*} This concludes the proof in one direction. Suppose now that for every bounded simple process $V$ with values in $\mathbb{R}_+$, $\mathbb{E}[(V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)_\infty] \ge 0$. To show that $X$ is a submartingale, let $s < t$ in $T$ and let $A = \{\mathbb{E}[X_t \mid \mathcal{F}_s] < X_s\} \in \mathcal{F}_s$. Define the simple process $V$ by $V_r = \mathbb{1}_A \mathbb{1}_{(s, t]}(r)$. Then \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{1}_A (X_t - X_s)] &= \mathbb{E}[(V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)_\infty] \ge 0 \: . \end{align*} But we also have \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{1}_A (X_t - X_s)] &= \mathbb{E}[\min\{\mathbb{E}[X_t \mid \mathcal{F}_s] - X_s, 0\}] \le 0 \: . \end{align*} Combining both inequalities, we get $\mathbb{E}[\min\{\mathbb{E}[X_t \mid \mathcal{F}_s] - X_s, 0\}] = 0$. Since $\min\{\mathbb{E}[X_t \mid \mathcal{F}_s] - X_s, 0\}$ is nonpositive and has expectation zero, it is almost surely zero. Thus $\mathbb{E}[X_t \mid \mathcal{F}_s] \ge X_s$ almost surely, which concludes the proof.
An adapted integrable process $X$ is a martingale if and only if for every bounded simple process $V$ with values in $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{E}[(V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)_\infty] = 0$.
nodes.label: lem:martingale_iff_integral_elemStochIntegral_eq_zero

nodes.statement: There might not be an order on the type $E$ of values of $X$, so we cannot just say that $X$ is a martingale if and only if both $X$ and $-X$ are submartingales and conclude with Lemma~\ref{lem:submartingale_iff_integral_elemStochIntegral_nonneg}. But we can use almost the same proof as in Lemma~\ref{lem:submartingale_iff_integral_elemStochIntegral_nonneg}, replacing inequalities by equalities?

Let $X$ be a submartingale and $A$ be an elementary predictable set. Then for all $t \in T$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{1}_A \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)_t] \le \mathbb{E}[X_t - X_0] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: cor:Submartingale.integral_elemStochIntegral_le

nodes.statement: Let $A$ be an elementary predictable set and let $t \in T$. \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{1}_A \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)_t] &= \mathbb{E}[X_t - X_0] - \mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{1}_{A^c} \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)_t] \le \mathbb{E}[X_t - X_0] \: . \end{align*} The inequality follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:submartingale_iff_integral_elemStochIntegral_nonneg} applied to the nonnegative bounded simple process $\mathbb{1}_{A^c}$.
Let $X$ be a submartingale and $V$ be a nonnegative bounded simple process. Then the elementary stochastic integral $V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X$ is a submartingale.
nodes.label: lem:Submartingale.elemStochIntegral

nodes.statement: We use Lemma~\ref{lem:submartingale_iff_integral_elemStochIntegral_nonneg} and have to show that for every nonnegative bounded simple process $W$, $\mathbb{E}[(W \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} (V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X))_\infty] \ge 0$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:elemStochIntegral_assoc}, this is $\mathbb{E}[((W \times V) \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)_\infty]$. Since $W \times V$ is a nonnegative bounded simple process, this is nonnegative by Lemma~\ref{lem:submartingale_iff_integral_elemStochIntegral_nonneg} applied to $X$.
Let $X$ be a martingale and $V$ be a bounded simple process. Then the elementary stochastic integral $V \bullet_B X$ is a martingale.
nodes.label: lem:Martingale.elemStochIntegral

nodes.statement: We use Lemma~\ref{lem:martingale_iff_integral_elemStochIntegral_eq_zero} and have to show that for every bounded simple process $W$, $\mathbb{E}[(W \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} (V \bullet_B X))_\infty] = 0$. By Lemma~\ref{cor:elemStochIntegral_assoc_real_bilin}, this is $\mathbb{E}[((W \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} V) \bullet_B X)_\infty]$. Since $W \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} V$ is a bounded simple process, this is zero by Lemma~\ref{lem:martingale_iff_integral_elemStochIntegral_eq_zero} applied to $X$.

nodes.name: Stochastic intervals
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be a time domain and let $\sigma, \tau$ be functions $\Omega \to T \cup \{\infty\}$. We define \begin{align*} [\![\sigma, \tau]\!] &= \{(t, \omega) \in T \times \Omega \mid \sigma(\omega) \le t \le \tau(\omega)\} \:, \\ [\![\sigma, \tau[\![ &= \{(t, \omega) \in T \times \Omega \mid \sigma(\omega) \le t < \tau(\omega)\} \:, \\ ]\!]\sigma, \tau]\!] &= \{(t, \omega) \in T \times \Omega \mid \sigma(\omega) < t \le \tau(\omega)\} \:, \\ ]\!]\sigma, \tau[\![ &= \{(t, \omega) \in T \times \Omega \mid \sigma(\omega) < t < \tau(\omega)\} \:, \\ [\![\sigma]\!] &= \{(t, \omega) \in T \times \Omega \mid \sigma(\omega) = t\} = [\![\sigma, \sigma]\!] \:. \end{align*} We call those stochastic intervals. Note that these are subsets of $T \times \Omega$, not of $ (T \cup \{\infty\}) \times \Omega$. $[\![\sigma]\!]$ is called the graph of $\sigma$.
nodes.label: def:stochasticInterval

nodes.statement: If $\sigma$ and $\tau$ are stopping times, then the stochastic interval $]\!]\sigma, \tau]\!]$ is a predictable set.
nodes.label: lem:predictable_stochasticInterval

nodes.statement: If $\sigma$ and $\tau$ are stopping times on $\mathbb{N}$, with $\tau$ bounded, then the stochastic interval $]\!]\sigma, \tau]\!]$ is an elementary predictable set.
nodes.label: lem:elementaryPredictableSet_stochasticInterval

nodes.statement: Let $n$ be an upper bound for $\tau$. To see that the stochastic interval is an elementary predictable set, note that it can be written as a finite disjoint union of sets \begin{align*} \{\sigma(\omega) < t \le \tau(\omega)\} &= \bigcup_{k=1}^{n} \{k\} \times \{\sigma < k \le \tau\} \\ &= \bigcup_{k=1}^{n} (k-1, k] \times \{\sigma \le k-1 < \tau\} \end{align*} where $\{\sigma \le k-1 < \tau\} \in \mathcal{F}_{k-1}$. Therefore this is an elementary predictable set.

Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a stochastic process, $t \in T$, and $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$. The auxiliary lower crossing time $\sigma'_{a, s, t}$ is the hitting time of the set $(-\infty, a]$ by the process $X$ between times $s$ and $t$.
nodes.label: def:lowerCrossingTimeAux

nodes.name: Upper crossing time
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a stochastic process, $t \in T$, and $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$. The $n$-th upper crossing time $\tau^n_{a, b, t}$ of the interval $[a, b]$ by $X$ before time $t$ is the hitting time of the set $[b, \infty)$ by $X$ after hitting the set $(-\infty, a]$ for the $n-1$-th time. That is, $\tau^0_{a, b, t} = 0$, and for all $n$, $\tau^{n+1}_{a, b, t}$ is the hitting time of $[b, \infty)$ by $X$ between $\sigma'_{a, \tau^{n}_{a, b, t}, t}$ and $t$.
nodes.label: def:upperCrossingTime

nodes.name: Lower crossing time
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a stochastic process, $t \in T$, and $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$. The $n$-th lower crossing time $\sigma^n_{a, b, t}$ of the interval $[a, b]$ by $X$ before time $t$ is the hitting time of the set $(-\infty, a]$ by $X$ after hitting the set $[b, \infty)$ for the $n$-th time. That is, it is the hitting time of $(-\infty, a]$ by $X$ between $\tau^n_{a, b, t}$ and $t$.
nodes.label: def:lowerCrossingTime

nodes.name: Upcrossings before time $t$
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a stochastic process, $t \in T$, and $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$. The number of upcrossings $U_t[a, b]$ of the interval $[a, b]$ by $X$ before time $t$ is the largest $n$ such that $\tau^n_{a, b, t} < t$, or $\infty$ if there is no such largest $n$.
nodes.label: def:upcrossingsBefore

nodes.name: Upcrossings
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a stochastic process and $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$. The number of upcrossings $U[a, b]$ of the interval $[a, b]$ by $X$ is the supremum over $t \in T$ of the number of upcrossings $U_t[a, b]$ of $[a, b]$ by $X$ before time $t$.
nodes.label: def:upcrossings

nodes.statement: Let $u : \beta \to \alpha$, for $\alpha$ a densely ordered, conditionally complete linear order equipped with the order topology. Let $S$ be a dense subset of $\alpha$ and $f$ a filter of $\beta$. If for all $a < b$ in $S$, the number of upcrossings of the interval $[a, b]$ by $u$ along $f$ is finite, then $u$ tends to a limit along $f$.
nodes.label: lem:tendsto_of_no_upcrossings

nodes.statement: For an adapted process $X : \mathbb{N} \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ indexed by the natural numbers, the upper crossing time $\tau^n_{a, b, t}$ is a stopping time.
nodes.label: lem:isStoppingTime_upperCrossingTime

nodes.statement: For an adapted process $X : \mathbb{N} \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ indexed by the natural numbers, the lower crossing time $\sigma^n_{a, b, t}$ is a stopping time.
nodes.label: lem:isStoppingTime_lowerCrossingTime

nodes.statement: Let $X : \mathbb{N} \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be an adapted process on the natural numbers. The upcrossing predictable set of $X$ before time $N$ is the predictable set defined by \begin{align*} A_N = \bigcup_{k=0}^{N-1} ]\!]\sigma^k_{a, b, N}, \tau^{k+1}_{a, b, N}]\!] \:. \end{align*}
nodes.label: def:upcrossingPredictableSet

nodes.statement: The upcrossing predictable set $A_N$ of $X : \mathbb{N} \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ before time $N$ is a predictable set.
nodes.label: lem:predictable_upcrossingPredictableSet

nodes.statement: By Lemmas \ref{lem:isStoppingTime_lowerCrossingTime} and \ref{lem:isStoppingTime_upperCrossingTime}, $\sigma^k_{a, b, N}$ and $\tau^{k+1}_{a, b, N}$ are stopping times. Hence by Lemma~\ref{lem:predictable_stochasticInterval}, the stochastic interval $]\!]\sigma^k_{a, b, N}, \tau^{k+1}_{a, b, N}]\!]$ is a predictable set for each $k$. Since a finite union of predictable sets is predictable, $A_N$ is predictable.
The upcrossing predictable set $A_N$ of $X : \mathbb{N} \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ before time $N$ is an elementary predictable set.
nodes.label: lem:elementaryPredictableSet_upcrossingPredictableSet

nodes.statement: By Lemmas \ref{lem:isStoppingTime_lowerCrossingTime} and \ref{lem:isStoppingTime_upperCrossingTime}, $\sigma^k_{a, b, N}$ and $\tau^{k+1}_{a, b, N}$ are stopping times, and are bounded by $N$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:elementaryPredictableSet_stochasticInterval}, the stochastic intervals $]\!]\sigma^k_{a, b, N}, \tau^{k+1}_{a, b, N}]\!]$ are elementary predictable sets for each $k$. Since a finite union of elementary predictable sets is elementary predictable, $A_N$ is elementary predictable.

Let $X : \mathbb{N} \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be an adapted process on the natural numbers. Then for all $a < b$ in $\mathbb{R}$ and $t \in \mathbb{N}$, for $A_t$ the upcrossing predictable set of $X$ before time $t$, the number of upcrossings $U_t[a, b]$ of the interval $[a, b]$ before time $t$ satisfies \begin{align*} (b - a) U_t[a, b] \le (\mathbb{1}_{A_t} \bullet X)_t + \max\{a - X_t, 0\} \:. \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:upcrossing_simpleProcess_le_nat

nodes.statement: \begin{align*} (\mathbb{1}_{A_t} \bullet X)_t &= \sum_{k=0}^t (X_{\tau^{k+1}_{a, b, t} \wedge t} - X_{\sigma^k_{a, b, t} \wedge t}) \\ &= \sum_{k=0}^{U_t[a, b]-1} (X_{\tau^{k+1}_{a, b, t} \wedge t} - X_{\sigma^k_{a, b, t} \wedge t}) + (X_t - X_{\sigma^{U_t[a, b]}_{a, b, t} \wedge t}) \\ &\ge (b - a) U_t[a, b] + \min\{X_t - a, 0\} \\ &= (b - a) U_t[a, b] - \max\{a - X_t, 0\} \: . \end{align*}

Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be an adapted process on a finite time domain $T$. Then for all $a < b$ in $\mathbb{R}$ and $t \in T$, there exists an elementary predictable set $A$ such that the number of upcrossings $U_t[a, b]$ of the interval $[a, b]$ before time $t$ satisfies \begin{align*} (b - a) U_t[a, b] \le (\mathbb{1}_A \bullet X)_t + \max\{a - X_t, 0\} \:. \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:upcrossing_simpleProcess_le

nodes.statement: Go from $T$ to a subset of $\mathbb{N}$ and use Lemma~\ref{lem:upcrossing_simpleProcess_le_nat}?

Let $T$ be a separable time domain, and let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be an adapted stochastic process such that $X$ is integrable and for every $t \in T$ the set $\{\mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{1}_A \bullet X)_t] \mid A \text{ elementary predictable}\}$ is bounded. Then $X$ has a modification $Y$ which has left and right limits everywhere and such that there is a countable set $S \subseteq T$ for which $Y$ is right-continuous on $T \setminus S$.
nodes.label: thm:exists_rightContinuous_modification_of_bounded_elemStochIntegral

nodes.statement:
Let $D$ be a countable dense subset of $T$ (e.g.\ the rationals in $T$) and let $t \in T$ and let $S$ be a finite subset of $D \cap [0, t]$. By Lemma~ef{lem:upcrossing_simpleProcess_le}, for all $a < b$ in $\mathbb{R}$, the number of upcrossings $U_S[a, b]$ of the interval $[a, b]$ along $S$ satisfies  egin{align*} (b - a) U_S[a, b] \le (\mathbb{1}_A  ullet X)_t + \max\{a - X_t, 0\} \end{align*} for some elementary predictable set $A$. Taking expectations and using the boundedness hypothesis, we obtain  egin{align*} (b - a) \mathbb{E}[U_S[a, b]] \le L + \mathbb{E}[\max\{a - X_t, 0\}] \le L + |a| + \mathbb{E}[|X_t|] \end{align*} where $L$ is a bound for $\{\mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{1}_A  ullet X)_t] \mid A 	ext{ elementary predictable}\}$. Now, let $S_1 \subseteq S_2 \subseteq \cdots$ be an increasing sequence of finite subsets of $D \cap [0, t]$ with $ igcup_n S_n = D \cap [0, t]$. The number of upcrossings $U_{S_n}[a, b]$ is increasing in $n$. By monotone convergence,  egin{align*} (b - a) \mathbb{E}[U_{D \cap [0, t]}[a, b]] = \lim_{n 	o \infty} (b - a) \mathbb{E}[U_{S_n}[a, b]] \le L + |a| + \mathbb{E}[|X_t|] < \infty. \end{align*} In particular, $U_{D \cap [0, t]}[a, b] < \infty$ a.s. for each pair $a < b$. Since $\mathbb{Q}^2$ is countable, we conclude that almost surely, for all rational $a < b$, the number of upcrossings of $[a, b]$ by $X$ along $D \cap [0, t]$ is finite. By Lemma~ef{lem:tendsto_of_no_upcrossings}, finite upcrossings of all rational intervals implies that the left and right limits of $s \mapsto X_s(\omega)$ along $D$ exist at every $t \in T$, for almost every $\omega$. Define $$	ilde{Y}_t(\omega) = \lim_{\substack{s \downarrow t \ s \in D}} X_s(\omega)$$ whenever this limit exists, and $	ilde{Y}_t(\omega) = 0$ otherwise. Then $	ilde{Y}$ has left and right limits everywhere (along $T$) almost surely, and is right-continuous at every point of $D$. We claim that the set  egin{align*} S = \{t \in T \mid 	ilde{Y}_t 
e X_t 	ext{ with positive probability}\} \end{align*} is countable. For each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, consider the set  egin{align*} S_n = \{t \in T \cap [0, n] \mid \mathbb{P}(|	ilde{Y}_t - X_t| > 1/n) > 1/n\} \:. \end{align*} We have $S =  igcup_n S_n$, so it suffices to show each $S_n$ is finite. If $S_n$ were infinite, it would contain a monotone sequence $t_k$ converging to some limit $t^* \in [0, n]$. Adding $\{t_k\}$ to $D$ and repeating the upcrossing argument, we would obtain that $X_{t_k}$ converges along $D \cup \{t_k\}$ almost surely. But $	ilde{Y}_{t_k}$ also converges (since $	ilde{Y}$ has left/right limits), giving $	ilde{Y}_{t_k} - X_{t_k} 	o 0$ in probability, contradicting the definition of $S_n$. Therefore each $S_n$ is finite and $S$ is countable. Define  egin{align*} Y_t =  egin{cases} X_t & 	ext{if } t \in S \:, \ 	ilde{Y}_t & 	ext{if } t 
otin S \:. \end{cases} \end{align*} Then $Y_t = X_t$ almost surely for all $t$: for $t \in S$ this is by definition, and for $t 
otin S$ this follows from $	ilde{Y}_t = X_t$ a.s. Thus $Y$ is a modification of $X$. Since $	ilde{Y}$ has left and right limits everywhere almost surely, and $Y$ differs from $	ilde{Y}$ only on the countable set $S$, $Y$ also has left and right limits everywhere almost surely. Furthermore, $Y$ agrees with $	ilde{Y}$ on $T \setminus S$, so $Y$ is right-continuous on $T \setminus S$.

Let $T$ be a separable time domain, and let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be an adapted stochastic process which is right-continuous in probability and such that the boundedness condition of Theorem~\ref{thm:exists_rightContinuous_modification_of_bounded_elemStochIntegral} holds. Then $X$ has a cadlag modification.
nodes.label: cor:exists_caldag_modification

nodes.statement: Let $Y$ be the modification of $X$ given by Theorem~\ref{thm:exists_rightContinuous_modification_of_bounded_elemStochIntegral}. $Y$ has left and right limits everywhere and there is a countable set $S$ such that $Y$ is right-continuous on $T \setminus S$. It remains to show that $Y$ is right-continuous at the points of $S$. Let $Y_{t+}$ denote the right limit of $Y$ at $t$. Since $X$ is right-continuous in probability, for all $t \in S$, $Y_t = Y_{t+}$ almost surely. Therefore, since $S$ is countable, we have that almost surely $Y_t = Y_{t+}$ for all $t \in S$ (and hence for all $t \in T$). $Y$ is therefore almost surely cadlag. We can modify $Y$ on the null set to obtain a cadlag modification of $X$.
Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a submartingale. Then for every $t \in T$, the set $\{\mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{1}_A \bullet X)_t] \mid A \text{ elementary predictable}\}$ is bounded.
nodes.label: lem:Submartingale.integral_elemStochIntegral_bounded

nodes.statement: Since $X$ is a submartingale, for any elementary predictable set $A$, we have (Corollary~\ref{cor:Submartingale.integral_elemStochIntegral_le}) \begin{align*} 0 \le \mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{1}_A \bullet X)_t] \le \mathbb{E}[X_t - X_0] \:. \end{align*} As $X_t$ and $X_0$ are integrable, the set $\{\mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{1}_A \bullet X)_t] \mid A \text{ elementary predictable}\}$ is bounded.
Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a submartingale which is right-continuous in probability. Then $X$ has a cadlag modification.
nodes.label: lem:Submartingale.exists_cadlag_modification_of_rightContinuous

nodes.statement: We apply Corollary~\ref{cor:exists_caldag_modification}, in which the boundedness condition of Theorem~\ref{thm:exists_rightContinuous_modification_of_bounded_elemStochIntegral} holds by Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.integral_elemStochIntegral_bounded}.

Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a submartingale. Then $X$ has a modification $Y$ such that for all $t \in T$, $Y$ has left and right limits at $t$ and such that there is a countable set $S \subseteq T$ for which $Y$ is right-continuous on $T \setminus S$.
nodes.label: lem:Submartingale.exists_modifications_limits

nodes.statement: Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:exists_rightContinuous_modification_of_bounded_elemStochIntegral}, in which the boundedness condition holds by Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.integral_elemStochIntegral_bounded}.

Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a submartingale and let $t_n$ be a decreasing sequence in $T$ which is bounded below. Then the family $\{X_{t_n}\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is uniformly integrable.
nodes.label: lem:Submartingale.uniformIntegrable_of_antitone_of_ge

nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a submartingale and $t \in T$. Let $t_n$ be a decreasing sequence in $T$ converging to $t$, and such that $X_{t_n}$ tends to a limit $X_{t+}$ almost surely. Then $X_t \le P[X_{t+} \mid \mathcal{F}_t]$ almost surely.
nodes.label: lem:Submartingale.le_condExp_of_tendsto

nodes.statement: By the submartingale property, for all $n$ we have that $X_t \le P[X_{t_n} \mid \mathcal{F}_t]$ almost surely. By Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.uniformIntegrable_of_antitone_of_ge}, the family $\{X_{t_n}\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is uniformly integrable. TODO: conclude that $P[X_{t+} \mid \mathcal{F}_t]$ is the limit of $P[X_{t_n} \mid \mathcal{F}_t]$.

Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a submartingale with respect to a right-continuous filtration. Then $X$ has a cadlag modification if and only if $t \mapsto \mathbb{E}[X_t]$ is right-continuous.
nodes.label: thm:Submartingale.exists_cadlag_modification_iff_rightContinuous

nodes.statement: Let $Y$ be the modification of $X$ given by Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.exists_modifications_limits}. $Y$ has left and right limits everywhere and there is a countable set $S$ such that $Y$ is right-continuous on $T \setminus S$. It remains to show that for each $t \in S$, $Y$ is right-continuous at $t$ almost surely. We will then be able to modify $Y$ on a null set to obtain a cadlag modification of $X$. Let $t \in S$ and let $Y_{t+}$ denote the right limit of $Y$ at $t$. We show that $Y_t = P[Y_{t+} \mid \mathcal{F}_t]$ almost surely, and that $P[Y_{t+} \mid \mathcal{F}_t] = Y_{t+}$ almost surely, which will conclude the proof. For the second equality it suffices to show that $Y_{t+}$ is $\mathcal{F}_t$-measurable, which follows from the right-continuity of the filtration. For the first equality, it suffices to show that $P[Y_{t+} \mid \mathcal{F}_t] - Y_t$ is an almost surely nonnegative random variable with zero expectation. Nonnegative follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.le_condExp_of_tendsto}. The expectation is $P[Y_{t+}] - P[Y_t]$. Let $t_n$ be a decreasing sequence in $T$ converging to $t$. By right-continuity of $t \mapsto \mathbb{E}[Y_t]$, we have that \begin{align*} P[Y_t] = \lim_{n \to \infty} P[Y_{t_n}] \: . \end{align*} By uniform integrability (Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.uniformIntegrable_of_antitone_of_ge}), we have that \begin{align*} P[Y_{t+}] = \lim_{n \to \infty} P[Y_{t_n}] \: . \end{align*} Therefore $P[Y_{t+}] = P[Y_t]$, which concludes the proof.
Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a martingale with respect to a right-continuous filtration. Then $X$ has a cadlag modification.
nodes.label: thm:Martingale.exists_cadlag_modification

nodes.statement: $X$ is in particular a submartingale, and for all $t \in T$, we have that $\mathbb{E}[X_t] = \mathbb{E}[X_0]$ by the martingale property. Therefore $t \mapsto \mathbb{E}[X_t]$ is right-continuous, and we can apply Theorem~\ref{thm:Submartingale.exists_cadlag_modification_iff_rightContinuous}.
Let the filtered probability space satisfy the usual conditions. Then every nonnegative submartingale $X$ admits a modification that is still a nonnegative submartingale with cadlag trajectories.
nodes.label: lem:exists_cadlag_mod_of_nonneg_submg

nodes.statement: See 8.2.3 of Pascucci.
Let the filtered probability space satisfy the usual conditions. Then every local martingale $X$ admits a modification that is still a local martingale with cadlag trajectories.
nodes.label: lem:exists_cadlag_mod_of_local_mg

nodes.statement: Let $(f_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in a vector space $E$ and $\phi : E \to \mathbb{R}_+$ be a function such that $\phi(f_n)$ is a bounded sequence. For $\delta > 0$, let $S_\delta = \{(f, g) \mid \phi(f)/2 + \phi(g)/2 - \phi((f+g)/2) \ge \delta\}$. Then there exist $g_n\in convex(f_n,f_{n+1},\cdots)$ such that for all $\delta > 0$, for $N$ large enough and $n, m \ge N$, $(g_n, g_m) \notin S_\delta$.
nodes.label: lem:komlos_convex

nodes.statement: Let $B$ be the bound of $(\phi(f_n))_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$. Then for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $g\in convex(f_n,f_{n+1},\cdots)$ we have $\phi(g)\le B$ by convexity of $\phi$. Let $r_n = \inf(\phi(g) \mid g\in convex(f_n, f_{n+1},\ldots))$. By construction $(r_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is nondecreasing. Let $A = \sup_{n \ge 1} r_n$, which is finite (as $A \le B$) and for each $n$ we may pick some $g_n\in convex(f_n, f_{n+1},\ldots)$ such that $\phi(g_n) \le A+1/n$ by $\inf$ and $\sup$ definitions. Let $\varepsilon \in (0, \delta/4)$. By properties of $\sup$ there exists $\bar{n}$ such that $r_{\bar{n}} \ge A-\varepsilon$ and such that $\frac{1}{\bar{n}} \le \varepsilon$. Let $m \ge k \ge \bar{n}$. We have $(g_k+g_m)/2 \in convex(f_k,f_{k+1},\ldots)$ and it follows since $(r_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is nondecreasing that $\phi((g_k+g_m)/2) \ge A - \varepsilon$. Hence due to the ordering of $m,k,\bar{n}$, \begin{align*} \phi(g_k)/2 + \phi(g_m)/2 - \phi((g_k+g_m)/2) &\le 2(A + \frac{1}{\bar{n}}) - 2(A - \varepsilon) \\ &\le 4 \varepsilon \\ &< \delta \: . \end{align*} Thus, for $n, m \ge \bar{n}$, $(g_n, g_m) \notin S_\delta$.
Let $H$ be a Hilbert space and $(f_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ a bounded sequence in $H$. Then there exist functions $g_n\in convex(f_n,f_{n+1},\cdots)$ such that $(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ converges in $H$.
nodes.label: lem:komlos_norm
